craft_claim: Periodic sentences and balanced antithesis slow the reading cadence so that an idea can be weighed rather than merely received.

supporting_evidence.location: On the Sublime, ch. 8 (sources of elevation) and chs. 16-23 (figures)
supporting_evidence.note: Pseudo-Longinus ties grandeur to elevated thought organised by figured composition, including the arrangement of clauses and the use of question and antithesis — the rhetorical ancestry of the philosophical cadence.

The repo's existing pacing claim already establishes syntax and rhythm as a control on reader tempo; the philosophical tone applies that control at the slower end. Cross-link, not independent support.

scope: Essayistic and academic prose, oratory, and contemplative passages in fiction.
exceptions: The cadence must yield at stakes-peaks; a periodic sentence over a crisis reads as stalling.
Acoustic claims about Greek or French rhythm require the original language and are not asserted here.
